newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi judge drops out of smoking case.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi judge drops out of smoking case.

text.p: A Mississippi judge accused of favoritism by tobacco industry lawyers on Wednesday removed himself from a $650 million secondhand-smoke case scheduled for trial in August.

Laurel County Circuit Court Judge Billy Joe Landrum said in a written order issued in Laurel that he was dropping out of the case he has overseen since 1994 and was asking the Mississippi Supreme Court to appoint a replacement.
It was not immediately clear what effect, if any, Landrum's decision would have on the timing of the trial, which had been scheduled to start on August 18, local attorneys said.
Two weeks ago, the state supreme court had stayed all proceedings in the case of barber Burl Butler pending resolution of the accusations against Landrum.
"The court is not prejudiced nor biased toward any party in this case ... but the court has now become an issue, rather than a judge in this case," Landrum wrote.

Tobacco industry attorneys fighting the claim by Bulter's family, which alleges the non-smoker's cancer death in 1994 was caused by secondhand smoke in his barbershop, said that Landrum had twice met privately with plaintiff lawyers.

The meetings did include representatives of Liggett, one of the defending tobacco companies in the case, but not the full contingent of tobacco defendants, and the meetings dealt with internal industry documents Liggett had released.

Liggett, a unit of Brooke Group, released the documents as part of a settlement with state attorneys general suing tobacco companies for Medicaid costs. Some government officials have described the Liggett papers as highly damaging to tobacco companies defending against some 1,000 lawsuits in the United States.
The meetings, the tobacco lawyers said, raised questions about Landrum's impartiality.
